book.t: In the Hebrew and Aramaic text, 4:1-3 is 3:31-33, and 4:4-37 is 4:1-34.

1:1.t: The third year of Jehoiakim was 605 BC, by Babylonian reckoning; Jeremiah 25:1 counts it as the fourth year.

1:7.t: The new Babylonian names honored Babylonian gods, replacing Hebrew names that honored the God of Israel: Daniel ("God is my judge"), Hananiah ("the LORD is gracious"), Mishael ("who is like God?"), Azariah ("the LORD helps").

1:11.t: "The steward": the KJV treats the word as a name, "Melzar"; the Hebrew hammeltsar is a title, "guardian".

1:12.t: "Vegetables": the KJV's "pulse", food grown from seed.

1:20.t: "Enchanters": the KJV's "astrologers"; the Hebrew ashshaphim are conjurers.

1:21.t: The first year of Cyrus was 539 BC, when Babylon fell. Daniel served through the whole exile.

2:4.t: "In Aramaic": the KJV's "in Syriack". From here to the end of chapter 7, Daniel is written in Aramaic, the international language of the empire.

2:5.t: "This is what I have firmly decided": the KJV's "The thing is gone from me", a misunderstanding of the Aramaic azda, "the word is firm".

2:46.t: Paying honor to Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar was honoring Daniel's God (verse 47).

3:1.t: "About 27 meters high and 2.7 meters wide": the KJV's "threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits".

3:2.t: "Satraps, prefects, governors, advisers, treasurers, judges, magistrates": the KJV's "princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs". Several of these Persian and Babylonian titles are uncertain.

3:5.t: "Horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe": the KJV's "cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer". The exact instruments are uncertain.

3:8.t: "Astrologers": the KJV's "Chaldeans", here a class of wise men.

3:21.t: "Robes, trousers, turbans": the KJV's "coats, their hosen, and their hats". The Aramaic words are uncertain.

3:25.t: "Like the Son of God": the KJV's reading. The Aramaic bar elahin can also mean "a son of the gods", that is, a divine being; verse 28 calls him God's angel.

4:17.t: "The Most High is sovereign over all kingdoms": the key message of the book. Human power is lent by God, and He can humble the proudest king.

5:1.t: Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, and ruled as co-regent. "His father Nebuchadnezzar" (verse 2) means his predecessor or ancestor.

5:7.t: "Purple": the KJV's "scarlet", the color of royalty. "The third highest ruler": after Nabonidus and Belshazzar himself.

5:25.t: Mene, Tekel and Peres are Aramaic weights (a mina, a shekel and a half-mina) and also verbs: "numbered", "weighed", "divided". Parsin is the plural of Peres, and Peres also sounds like "Persia". The KJV's "UPHARSIN" includes u, "and".

5:30.t: Babylon fell to the Persians in October 539 BC.

5:31.t: Darius the Mede is not named outside Daniel; he may be another name for Cyrus or for a governor he appointed. In the Aramaic text this verse is 6:1, and 6:1-28 is 6:2-29.

6:1.t: "Satraps": the KJV's "princes", provincial governors of the Persian empire.

7:1.t: The first year of Belshazzar was about 553 BC. Daniel 7 parallels the statue of chapter 2: four kingdoms, followed by the everlasting kingdom of God.

7:25.t: "A time, times and half a time": the KJV's "a time and times and the dividing of time", usually understood as three and a half years. Compare 12:7 and Revelation 12:14.

8:1.t: With chapter 8 the book returns to Hebrew.

8:2.t: "Susa": the KJV's "Shushan", a royal city of Persia. "The Ulai Canal": the KJV's "the river of Ulai".

8:9.t: "The Beautiful Land": the KJV's "the pleasant land", Israel.

8:12.t: "The host of the saints": the KJV's "an host". The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.

8:14.t: "2,300 evenings and mornings": the KJV's "two thousand and three hundred days". The Hebrew is literally "evening morning", which may mean 2,300 days or 1,150 days of evening and morning sacrifices.

8:20.t: The ram is the Medo-Persian empire; the goat is Greece; the first great horn is Alexander the Great (died 323 BC); the four horns are the four kingdoms into which his empire was divided.

8:23.t: The "fierce-looking king" is widely identified with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC.

9:1.t: "Xerxes": the KJV's "Ahasuerus". The first year of Darius was 539-538 BC.

9:24.t: "Seventy weeks": literally "seventy sevens", usually understood as seventy periods of seven years, 490 years.

9:27.t: "On a wing of the temple he will set up an abomination that causes desolation": the KJV's "for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate". The Hebrew is difficult. Jesus speaks of "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet" (Matthew 24:15).

10:1.t: "It concerned a great war": the KJV's "the time appointed was long". The third year of Cyrus was 536 BC.

10:4.t: "The Tigris": the KJV's "Hiddekel", its Hebrew name.

11:2.t: A detailed outline of the wars between the "king of the South" (the Ptolemies of Egypt) and the "king of the North" (the Seleucids of Syria) after Alexander the Great (verse 3). Verses 21-35 describe Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC. Many interpreters see verses 36-45 as moving beyond Antiochus to a final opponent of God at the end of the age.

11:30.t: "Ships of the western coastlands": the KJV's "the ships of Chittim", here the Romans.

11:31.t: "The temple fortress": the KJV's "the sanctuary of strength".

12:4.t: "Many will go here and there to increase knowledge": the KJV's "many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased".

12:7.t: "A time, times and half a time": the KJV's "a time, times, and an half", usually understood as three and a half years; see 7:25.

12:13.t: "You will rise to receive your allotted inheritance": the KJV's "stand in thy lot at the end of the days".

2:18.t: "Mystery" (Aramaic raz): a secret that only God can reveal. The Greek mysterion in the New Testament has the same meaning: something once hidden that God has now made known (Romans 16:25-26, Ephesians 3:3-6).

2:34.t: "A rock ... cut out, but not by human hands": a kingdom from God, not built by human effort, that grows to fill the earth and lasts forever. Jesus proclaimed "the kingdom of God" and called Himself the rejected stone that becomes the capstone (Matthew 21:42-44, Luke 20:17-18).

2:44.t: "A rock ... cut out, but not by human hands": a kingdom from God, not built by human effort, that grows to fill the earth and lasts forever. Jesus proclaimed "the kingdom of God" and called Himself the rejected stone that becomes the capstone (Matthew 21:42-44, Luke 20:17-18).

3:17.t: "Even if He does not": the three men trusted God's power to save them, but their faithfulness did not depend on being rescued. Hebrews 11:34 remembers those who "quenched the fury of the flames".

4:25.t: "The Most High is sovereign over all kingdoms": the key message of the book. Human power is lent by God, and He can humble the proudest king.

4:32.t: "The Most High is sovereign over all kingdoms": the key message of the book. Human power is lent by God, and He can humble the proudest king.

4:27.t: "Renounce your sins by doing what is right" (Aramaic tsidqah): righteousness here includes generosity to the poor. Compare Proverbs 14:31.

6:10.t: "Windows opened toward Jerusalem": Daniel prayed facing the city and its ruined temple, as Solomon had asked (1 Kings 8:46-50).

6:22.t: "My God sent His angel, and He shut the mouths of the lions": Hebrews 11:33 remembers those who "shut the mouths of lions" by faith. "I was found innocent": Daniel's integrity is the point of the story, both before God and before the king.

7:9.t: "The Ancient of Days" (Aramaic attiq yomin): God as the eternal Judge. Revelation 1:13-14 uses the same description, white hair like wool, for the risen Christ.

7:13.t: "One like the Son of Man" (Aramaic kevar enash): literally "one like a human being". He comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom and the worship of all peoples. Jesus took "the Son of Man" as His favorite title and quoted this verse at His trial (Mark 14:62). Following this reading, His pronouns are capitalized.

7:18.t: "The holy people of the Most High" (Aramaic qaddishe elyonin): the KJV's "the saints of the most High". God's people share the kingdom given to the Son of Man.

7:22.t: "The holy people of the Most High" (Aramaic qaddishe elyonin): the KJV's "the saints of the most High". God's people share the kingdom given to the Son of Man.

7:27.t: "The holy people of the Most High" (Aramaic qaddishe elyonin): the KJV's "the saints of the most High". God's people share the kingdom given to the Son of Man.

8:16.t: "Gabriel": the first angel named in the Bible. He later announced the births of John the Baptist and Jesus (Luke 1:19, 26).

9:4.t: "Who keeps His covenant of steadfast love" (Hebrew shomer habberit vehahesed): the KJV's "keeping the covenant and mercy". Daniel's prayer appeals not to Israel's merit but to God's hesed and His own name (verses 18-19).

9:25.t: "The Messiah, the Prince ... the Messiah will be cut off, but not for Himself" (Hebrew mashiach nagid ... yikkaret mashiach ve'en lo): the KJV's reading. Mashiach means "anointed one". Christians have long read this as the coming and death of Jesus, who was "cut off" for others. The Hebrew ve'en lo can also mean "and will have nothing". Following the KJV's reading, the Messiah's pronouns are capitalized.

10:13.t: "Michael ... your prince": an archangel who guards God's people (12:1, Jude 9, Revelation 12:7). The "prince of Persia" and "prince of Greece" are spiritual powers behind earthly empires. Compare Ephesians 6:12.

10:21.t: "Michael ... your prince": an archangel who guards God's people (12:1, Jude 9, Revelation 12:7). The "prince of Persia" and "prince of Greece" are spiritual powers behind earthly empires. Compare Ephesians 6:12.

11:32.t: "The people who know their God will firmly resist him": faithfulness under persecution is the mark of God's people. Hebrews 11:35-38 may recall the martyrs of this period.

12:1.t: "Everyone whose name is found written in the book": the book of life. See Exodus 32:32, Psalm 69:28, Luke 10:20 and Revelation 20:12-15.

12:2.t: "Multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake: some to everlasting life" (Hebrew chayye olam): the clearest statement in the Old Testament of a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. "Everlasting life" appears here for the first time in Scripture. Jesus echoes this verse in John 5:28-29.
